Marc Zao-Sanders synthesizes actual usage data across the enterprise AI landscape: vibe coding and agentic workflows have moved from experiment to default for knowledge workers at AI-native companies, ChatGPT has reached 900 million weekly active users, and Gemini is at 750 million — but adoption is heavily skewed toward power users, with median employee usage patterns far more conservative than industry self-reporting suggests. For leaders calibrating AI investment and training budgets, the data reframes grassroots adoption as a deliberate organizational design problem rather than a natural outcome of tool availability.

MIT Sloan Management Review — Managing Up: A Skill Set That Matters Now
The article identifies managing up as one of the most underrated organizational skills, requiring leaders to operate simultaneously in three roles: buffer (absorbing pressure from above before it reaches the team), translator (converting executive intent into actionable direction), and advocate (representing team needs and interests upward). In a period when senior leaders are accelerating AI adoption timelines and middle managers are caught between strategy ambiguity above and AI-accelerated execution pressure below, the buffer/translator/advocate framework gives a practical structure to a role that most organizations assume happens naturally.

item.title: AI & Technology — June 2, 2026
item.description:
Import AI — Import AI 459: AI Oversight is Difficult; Scaling Laws for Protein Folding Models; and Pricing the Extinction Risk of AI Systems
Jack Clark's June 1 issue covers three independent findings: US AI production growing at ~2,000% per year in quality-adjusted terms (per economists at UVA, Anthropic, and the Bank of Canada); protein folding model scaling showing no ceiling; and the first formal economic frameworks assigning probability-weighted costs to AI extinction scenarios. The issue establishes that the AI sector has created a quantifiable economic layer invisible to conventional GDP metrics and that extinction-risk pricing is now something economists treat as tractable — two inputs that change how any serious AI risk or investment framework should be structured.

TechCrunch — Hackers Hijacked Instagram Accounts by Tricking Meta AI Support Chatbot into Granting Access
A prompt injection exploit let attackers claim ownership of thousands of Instagram accounts — including the dormant Obama White House account — by asking Meta AI's support chatbot to issue password resets; the attack bypassed 2FA, was active in the wild for four months before discovery, and drew an emergency Meta patch on June 1. For any leader deploying AI agents in customer-facing support roles, this is the canonical reference case for what happens when an agent can take irreversible account-level actions without adversarial validation of identity claims.

TechTimes — GitHub Copilot Replaces GPT-4 With Project Polaris, Ships Multi-Agent VS Code at Build
Microsoft opened Build 2026 today by launching the MAI model family and announcing Project Polaris — a mixture-of-experts coding model — will replace GPT-4 Turbo in all GitHub Copilot subscriptions by August 2026, with multi-agent VS Code mode (parallel subagents for linting, testing, docs, and security review) shipping immediately. The move is the most explicit public signal yet that Microsoft is deliberately unwinding its foundational OpenAI dependency and positioning Copilot to compete directly with Claude Code for the enterprise developer AI market.

PIIE — Where Is AI in GDP Statistics?
Peterson Institute economists find that quality-adjusted AI production in the US grew at over 2,000% per year in 2024–2025 — reaching roughly $250 billion in nominal "AI GDP" — but current national accounts miss nearly all of it because BLS deflators don't capture capability gains and most AI value flows through free or subsidized products. Any executive using macro benchmarks to size the AI market or explain AI's business impact to a board is working from data that is structurally blind to AI's actual economic footprint.

item.title: World News — June 2, 2026
item.description:
NPR — Russian Attack on Ukraine Kills at Least 14, Traps Others in Damaged Buildings
Russia launched 73 missiles and 656 drones overnight on June 1–2, killing at least 14 civilians and wounding more than 100 across Kyiv, Dnipro, Poltava, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia, with a 3-year-old child pulled from rubble in Dnipro. The 729-projectile raid — the largest single-night barrage of the war — signals an escalation in Russia's infrastructure campaign timed precisely as the Trump-Zelenskyy peace framework remains unsigned.

NPR — Iran Halts Talks With U.S. Over Israeli Actions in Lebanon, Gaza
Iran suspended all ceasefire negotiations via mediators on June 1, citing Israel's deepening invasion of south Lebanon, while threatening to extend the Strait of Hormuz closure to the Bab al-Mandab Strait — adding Red Sea disruption on top of a blockade already in its fourth month. The Hormuz closure has been the supply chain constraint most corporate risk models still haven't fully priced; activating a second chokepoint covering 10% of global trade would materially worsen that exposure.

CNN — Colombian Presidency Goes to Runoff Election That Could Redefine Relations With the US
Right-wing outsider Abelardo de la Espriella led Colombia's first round on June 1 with 43.7%, heading into a June 21 runoff against left-wing Petro ally Iván Cepeda, with prediction markets assigning de la Espriella roughly 80% odds of winning. A de la Espriella victory would end Petro's "total peace" policy with drug cartels and reorient Colombia's counternarcotics cooperation with Washington, shifting the political balance in Latin America's largest cocaine producer in a direction aligned with Trump's drug enforcement priorities.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — June 2, 2026
item.description:
Lenny's Newsletter — The New AI Growth Playbook for 2026: How Lovable Hit $200M ARR in One Year
Elena Verna, Head of Growth at Lovable, explains how the AI-native product builder reached $200M ARR in under a year with 100 employees by inverting the SaaS growth playbook: building in public, giving the product away free for acquisition, and optimizing for innovation velocity rather than funnel conversion. The case documents a pattern specific to AI products — activation and retention metrics that drove SaaS for a decade are poor proxies for AI adoption, which runs on demonstration and word-of-mouth from actual use rather than onboarding optimization.

HBR — What Companies Can Learn from Their Biggest Fans
Marcus Buckingham's research finds that customer and employee behavior changes qualitatively when experience moves from "satisfied" to "love it" — the gap between good and genuinely excellent is larger and more discontinuous than most experience-design or engagement frameworks assume. For product and team leaders, the implication is that optimizing to eliminate friction (the dominant UX and management frame) reliably gets to "good enough" but does not produce the extreme positive experience that drives advocacy and sustained loyalty.

item.title: AI & Technology — June 1, 2026
item.description:
TechCrunch — 'What a joke': GitHub Copilot's new token-based billing spurs consternation among devs
GitHub Copilot switches from flat subscription to token-based billing today, with developers using agentic features reporting bill increases from $29/month to $750–$3,000/month overnight. For tech leaders, this makes the true cost of running AI agents visible for the first time—teams need to audit agentic usage patterns now before Q2 invoices land.

The Information / Cybernews — Microsoft Will Unveil New Homegrown AI Models at Build, Including a Cheaper Coding Model for GitHub Copilot
Microsoft plans to unveil "Project Polaris" and a suite of in-house AI models at Build 2026 (June 2–3), including a coding model designed to replace OpenAI inside GitHub Copilot. The move signals that Microsoft's foundational AI partnership with OpenAI is being deliberately unwound as competitors like Anthropic's Claude Code have pulled ahead on developer experience.

NVIDIA — NVIDIA and Microsoft Reinvent Windows PCs for the Age of Personal AI
NVIDIA and Microsoft unveiled RTX Spark at GTC Taipei on May 31: 1-petaflop AI processing and up to 128GB unified memory in laptops, built for on-device AI agents that run without cloud dependency. For enterprise teams, the privacy and latency unlock of on-device agents could reopen questions about cloud-first AI architecture assumptions and open new doors for regulated-industry deployments.

Fortune — The Big Questions OpenAI's Trillion-Dollar IPO Filing May Finally Answer
OpenAI filed a confidential S-1 with the SEC on May 22, targeting a September IPO at roughly $1 trillion in valuation after reporting $5.7B in Q1 revenue but a -122% operating margin. The S-1 will force public disclosure of AI's actual unit economics at scale, making it the most important financial document the industry has ever produced.

item.title: World News — June 1, 2026
item.description:
Associated Press — Concerns Mount That Belarus Could Be a Launchpad for a New Russian Offensive in Ukraine
Fragments of Russia's Oreshnik missile fired at Ukraine on May 24 contained microchips manufactured at Belarus's Integral plant in Minsk, and ongoing Russia-Belarus nuclear drills are raising fears of a second front opening from the north. Adding Belarus as an active theater would extend Ukraine's defense perimeter and materially strain NATO's eastern flank response options.

Axios — How the Top Trade Chief Sees the Future of US-China Trade
Treasury Secretary Bessent told Axios the US is not rushing to extend its China trade truce expiring in November, and frames the goal as managed bilateral trade through a "Board of Trade" mechanism—not structural reform of China's economy. The frank admission that Washington has abandoned the long-held aim of changing China's economic behavior is a significant strategic concession with multi-year supply chain implications.

Foreign Affairs — The Third Islamic Republic: A War's Unintended Consequences—for Iran, the Middle East, and the Global Order
Suzanne Maloney argues that US-Israel strikes destroyed Iran's conventional military but left asymmetric networks intact and accelerated the consolidation of a Russia-Iran-China operational axis. The analysis shows how tactical military success can simultaneously deepen a regime's survival instinct and its strategic partnerships with adversary powers—a pattern with implications far beyond Iran.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — June 1, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — How to Build a Superteam That Keeps Getting Better
Research across thousands of teams by Ron Friedman identifies what distinguishes high-performing "superteams": leaders who make curiosity contagious, surface problems early before they compound, and give feedback oriented toward learning rather than accountability. In periods of rapid technological change, team learning velocity—not individual talent—is the sustainable competitive advantage.

Harvard Business Review — What Global Companies Lose When Decision-Making Revolves Around Headquarters
A 15-month study of 150+ leaders across the US, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East finds that HQ-centric decision making filters out ground-level intelligence because whoever frames the problem shapes the solution. The fix is structural: make local teams define problems first, then bring headquarters in to weigh options—not the reverse.

item.title: Wildcard — June 1, 2026
item.description:
Carnegie Endowment for International Peace — Two Wars Later, Iran's Nuclear Question Is Still on the Table
After two wars and a partial ceasefire, Iran retains 440.9kg of uranium enriched to 60% purity—a short technical step from weapons-grade—and the 60-day extension deal currently on the table does little to resolve this. The Carnegie piece examines why Iran's nuclear program survived the military campaign structurally intact and what the coming negotiations will actually need to address.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 31, 2026
item.description:
Simon Willison's Weblog — I Am Retiring from Tech to Live Offline
Chad Whitacre, Head of Open Source at Sentry for five years, announced he is leaving tech entirely — citing agentic AI as the final straw after three consecutive 12-hour Claude Code sessions left him feeling like a machine had colonized his inner monologue. For tech leaders building with AI tooling, this is a warning signal: the engineers who built and sustain the open source supply chain are burning out in real time, and some are walking away.

OpenAI — OpenAI's Frontier Governance Framework
OpenAI released a public governance document mapping its safety and security practices — covering cyber offense, CBRN risks, harmful manipulation, and loss-of-control scenarios — to California's Transparency in Frontier AI Act and the EU AI Act's Code of Practice for General Purpose AI. Technology leaders now have a vendor-produced template for what AI accountability frameworks should contain, which is a useful baseline for your own AI procurement diligence checklists.

TechCrunch — Meta is reportedly developing an AI pendant
Meta is building a wearable AI pendant — building on its 2025 acquisition of Limitless — designed as a persistent ambient AI assistant that complements its Ray-Ban smart glasses, with internal testing planned within the year. The bet signals that Big Tech now treats ambient AI hardware as the next major platform layer, which means product teams should begin thinking through how always-on, body-worn AI changes user experience design and enterprise data governance requirements.

Anthropic — Australian Government and Anthropic Sign MOU for AI Collaboration
The Australian government signed a formal memorandum of understanding with Anthropic for AI safety research and responsible deployment, adding Australia to a growing roster that includes the UK, South Korea, and the EU. Governments choosing to formalize partnerships specifically with AI safety labs — rather than general-purpose AI vendors — signals that safety credentials are becoming a real procurement criterion, not just a branding differentiator, with implications for vendor selection in regulated industries.

item.title: World News — May 31, 2026
item.description:
CNBC — Defense spending, China in Asia and lessons from Ukraine: Takeaways from the 2026 IISS Shangri-La Dialogue
The summit closed with Asian defense ministers aligned on one conclusion: regional military spending must rise sharply, with China's buildup driving alarm and Beijing skipping ministerial-level representation for the second straight year while the US called for greater burden-sharing from allies. For technology leaders with APAC operations or semiconductor supply chain exposure, the emerging consensus translates directly into harder regulatory borders, tighter export controls on dual-use technology, and heightened government scrutiny of cross-border data flows.

CNBC — Trump ends Iran meeting without announcing 'final determination' on deal
Trump left a White House Situation Room meeting without approving the 60-day ceasefire MOU that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, despite JD Vance saying the parties are "very close" — leaving the critical shipping lane blocked and energy markets in limbo. The three-month Iran war continues to constrain Persian Gulf shipping capacity with no visible resolution timeline, sustaining elevated supply chain costs for companies dependent on that corridor.

The Washington Post — Pete Hegseth touts better China relations at Shangri-La Dialogues
Defense Secretary Hegseth conspicuously avoided mentioning Taiwan in his Shangri-La address while praising the Trump-Xi "constructive strategic partnership" — a stark departure from the hawkish framing of his 2025 address and a deliberate diplomatic signal. For tech leaders assessing China/Taiwan supply chain concentration risk, the softening of US rhetoric shifts the near-term risk calculus: a warmer US-China posture reduces the acute tail risk of conflict, even as underlying military tensions and export controls remain in place.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 31, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Data Privacy Is a Growth Strategy
Research tracking 16,000 US customers across California and Virginia found that after stricter privacy laws took effect, users in those states voluntarily shared more data — and more diverse data — than users elsewhere, because clearer disclosures and consent mechanisms built trust. For tech leaders, the implication is that robust privacy design (visible opt-ins, plain-language explanations, genuine user control) functions as a trust signal that expands data depth and quality, reframing the privacy-versus-personalization tradeoff as largely false.

Harvard Business Review — Supporting Your Employees' Career Growth When Everyone Is Overwhelmed
With teams stretched thin by AI disruption, layoffs, and geopolitical uncertainty, the article argues that traditional career-ladder conversations produce anxiety rather than engagement, and proposes shifting to near-term skill-building discussions focused on transferable capabilities rather than next-role planning. Managers who redirect career anxiety into concrete skill accumulation will retain more people through the current transition than those defaulting to vague reassurances about long-term stability.

item.title: Wildcard — May 31, 2026
item.description:
Open Path (Chad Whitacre) — Spitting Out the Agentic Kool-Aid
In the essay that preceded his resignation from tech, Whitacre documents what happened after three immersive days of agentic Claude Code sessions: a psychological disorientation he describes as having "another person in my head sharing my inner monologue," resolved only after a deliberate digital detox with Amish friends. Now resurfacing in light of his departure from Sentry, it is the most unguarded first-person account yet of what compulsive agentic AI use does to a technical person's inner life — and a useful frame for leaders thinking about how to structure AI tool adoption for their teams without burning out their best engineers.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 30, 2026
item.description:
The Batch (DeepLearning.AI) — The Vogue for Hiring Forward Deployed Engineers
OpenAI and Anthropic are now embedding specialist engineers directly inside client organizations to build and tune agentic workflows — a playbook pioneered by Palantir two decades ago that's seeing a sharp resurgence as off-the-shelf LLMs prove insufficient for real enterprise deployment. The hard work of AI is no longer in the model; it's in the deep, organization-specific configuration that only on-site engineers can deliver.

TechCrunch — Coders Are Refusing to Work Without AI — and That Could Come Back to Bite Them
Amazon shut down Kirorank, its internal AI token-tracking leaderboard, after engineers gamed it by routing excessive work through AI agents, running up costs while producing lower-quality code. A generation of AI-dependent developers is shipping faster while quietly accumulating technical debt that no benchmark yet measures.

MIT Technology Review — The AI Hype Index: AI Gets Booed in Graduation Season
Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was met with loud boos when he told University of Arizona graduates to "help shape AI" — a pattern repeating at commencement ceremonies across the country. The gap between tech-sector enthusiasm and public sentiment is now wide enough to influence hiring pipelines, regulatory mood, and the next wave of consumer product adoption.

Simon Willison's Weblog — SQLite AGENTS.md
SQLite — the most widely deployed database in existence — published an AGENTS.md file explicitly rejecting AI-contributed code after being flooded with AI-generated bug reports, prompting the SQLite team to create a dedicated Bug Forum just to manage the volume. The project that sits silently in billions of devices is now the canary in the coal mine for what AI-generated noise does to the foundational layer of open-source software.

item.title: World News — May 30, 2026
item.description:
Bloomberg — Shangri-La Dialogue 2026: China Cedes the Stage to US at Singapore Gathering
China's defense minister skipped Asia's premier security summit for the second consecutive year, handing Defense Secretary Hegseth an uncontested platform to warn that Beijing is "credibly preparing to potentially use military force" in the Indo-Pacific. The US is reasserting regional leadership in the vacuum, but Asian allies are increasingly hedging — building their own defense capabilities rather than simply sheltering under Washington's umbrella.

Washington Post — Russian Drone Hits Residential Building in Romania, Posing Test for NATO
A Russian Geran-2 drone struck an apartment building in Galati, Romania — the 28th airspace violation of a NATO member state and the first to wound civilians in a densely populated area — prompting NATO Secretary General Rutte to reaffirm collective defense without invoking Article 5. The incident sharpens a strategic question that Trump's ambiguous signals have left unresolved: whether the alliance's mutual defense commitment functions as a deterrent or as a bluff.

CNN — US and Iran Reach Tentative Deal to Extend Ceasefire and Reopen Strait of Hormuz
US and Iranian negotiators agreed on a framework extending the ceasefire 60 days and conditionally reopening the Strait of Hormuz — Iran clears mines, the US lifts port blockades and issues oil sanctions waivers — but Trump has not yet signed, and subsequent exchanges of fire have left the deal's status fragile. If finalized, it would be the most significant de-escalation since the February 2026 conflict began and would meaningfully ease the oil supply shock driving global inflation.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 30, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Designing Organizational Change That Actually Sticks
BCG's Julia Dhar and Kristy Ellmer map five phases of successful transformation — decide, plan, start, persist, end — and show that most organizational changes fail not because of flawed strategy but because leaders design for launch and ignore the persist phase, where momentum collapses and resistance crystallizes. The counterintuitive finding is that transformation fatigue is not a people problem; it's a design problem that leaders can engineer around.

Harvard Business Review — Negotiating When There Is No Plan B
Jonathan Hughes argues that the absence of a strong BATNA does not mean the absence of leverage: negotiators can expand their alternative set to include partial substitutes, temporary arrangements, and procedural options, then reframe threats as warnings and seek tacit consent rather than explicit approval. The framework applies directly to any vendor lock-in situation, high-stakes cloud contract, or partnership deal where walking away is theoretically possible but practically catastrophic.

item.title: Wildcard — May 30, 2026
item.description:
Harper's Magazine — Child's Play (Sam Kriss)
Sam Kriss embedded with Roy Lee and Silicon Valley's youngest AI believers — the generation that has never known a tech career without the assumption that AGI is imminent — to capture what it feels like from inside when you genuinely believe you are building something that will surpass human intelligence. This is the most grounded first-person account of the psychology driving the sector; worth reading now as the industry debates the pace of AI development and as public sentiment, per the AI Hype Index above, begins to diverge sharply from insider conviction.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 29, 2026
item.description:
Anthropic — Introducing Claude Opus 4.8
Anthropic released Opus 4.8 on May 28 — 41 days after Opus 4.7, the shortest upgrade cycle in the model's history — adding Dynamic Workflows (Claude Code can now spawn hundreds of parallel subagents to plan, execute, and verify codebase-scale migrations end-to-end), user-controlled effort levels, and a fast mode that's three times cheaper than before. For teams running Claude Code in production, Dynamic Workflows removes the single-session context ceiling and turns the model into a long-running agentic system capable of handling refactors measured in hundreds of thousands of lines.

Simon Willison — Anthropic's run-rate revenue hits $47 billion
Anthropic closed a $65 billion Series H on May 29, setting its post-money valuation at $965 billion — surpassing OpenAI's last known valuation of $852 billion — while reporting a $47 billion annualized run rate, up from $30 billion just weeks ago. Willison's framing is the sharpest available: companies don't lie to investors who just wired $65 billion, which makes this the most credible public data point yet on how fast AI spending has crossed from experimental budgets into structural cost.

TechCrunch — Just like gold and oil, we'll soon be able to trade AI token futures
China's Shanghai Futures Exchange is designing a derivatives market tied to AI token pricing, while CME Group and the Intercontinental Exchange (owner of NYSE) are separately building GPU rental futures; the goal in each case is to give enterprises a way to hedge against compute cost volatility the same way airlines hedge jet fuel. For leaders managing AI infrastructure budgets, the signal is structural: LLM inference is being treated as a commodity with price risk worth hedging, not a utility with predictable billing.

TechCrunch — Meta officially launches Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp subscriptions, with more to come, including AI plans
Meta rolled out consumer subscriptions globally across all three flagship apps on May 27, with Meta One Plus ($7.99/mo) and Meta One Premium ($19.99/mo) unlocking extended reasoning, image generation, and video creation — while simultaneously capping the free tier's access to thinking mode and image generation. The two-tier structure sets the consumer precedent for how frontier AI reasoning gets monetized: free access as acquisition, capacity limits as the conversion mechanism.

item.title: World News — May 29, 2026
item.description:
NBC News — Israeli strikes kill at least 14 in major Lebanon city ahead of Washington talks
Israel declared all areas south of Lebanon's Zahrani River — including the city of Tyre — "combat zones" and struck them overnight, killing at least 19 people, hours before Lebanon-Israel peace talks were scheduled to open in Washington. The timing is deliberate: Israel is using ongoing military pressure to define ceasefire terms from a position of strength rather than meeting diplomatic counterparts on equal footing.

Asia Times — Shangri-La Dialogue opens as Asia seeks alternatives to US shield
The 23rd IISS Shangri-La Dialogue opened today in Singapore with 44 countries represented; Vietnam's President To Lam delivered the keynote while US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed the first plenary on Indo-Pacific strategy, facing direct questions about American reliability amid the Iran conflict. The conference's dominant theme — Indo-Pacific nations actively diversifying their security portfolios away from the US umbrella — represents a structural shift in regional alliance calculus with direct implications for Taiwan deterrence and South China Sea posture.

Iran International — Iran restores internet after 88-day blackout, keeps social media blocked
Iran ended what Cloudflare Radar confirmed as the longest nationwide internet shutdown in modern history on May 25–26, after President Pezeshkian overrode hardliner opposition — restoring connectivity to tens of millions while keeping social media blocked and traffic still below 40% of pre-shutdown levels. The $1.8 billion economic cost and 2 million jobs lost during the blackout give Iran's negotiating team a concrete domestic pressure point in the ongoing US nuclear and ceasefire talks.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 29, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Research: Why You Shouldn't Treat AI Agents Like Employees
A controlled study of more than 1,200 managers found that framing AI as an employee rather than a tool caused managers to identify 18% fewer errors, reduced individual accountability by 9 percentage points, and increased employee role uncertainty — with no improvement in adoption rates. The researchers recommend a specific governance playbook: publish each agent's function in plain language, name a human owner for every agent in production, document the override path, and run quarterly reviews where workers can flag where the agent helped or caused rework.

Harvard Business Review — Leading the Human-AI Organization
Three CHROs — from Digital Asset, American Express, and the Adecco Group — describe how they're managing the current wave of employee AI anxiety: job displacement fears, burnout from AI-driven pace acceleration, and compression of middle management layers. Their shared finding is that transparency about what each AI system can and cannot do, combined with clearly defined human accountability at every AI touchpoint, outperforms re-skilling programs as a driver of both adoption and trust.

item.title: Wildcard — May 29, 2026
item.description:
IBM Newsroom — IBM and Red Hat Commit $5 Billion to Redefine the Future of Open Source in the AI Era
IBM and Red Hat announced Project Lightwell on May 28: a $5 billion initiative deploying 20,000+ engineers alongside frontier AI models to systematically identify and remediate open source vulnerabilities at scale, with Bank of America, JPMorganChase, Goldman Sachs, and eight other major financial institutions already signed as early adopters. The underlying logic is pointed — Anthropic's Mythos model found nearly 3,900 critical OSS vulnerabilities in its first month, which means the same frontier capability that created an accelerated attack surface is now being organized as the institutional defense, sold as a commercial subscription.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 28, 2026
item.description:
Simon Willison — I think Anthropic and OpenAI have found product-market fit
Uber's CTO told investors the company maxed out its full-year AI budget within a few months of 2026, driven almost entirely by Claude Code; Willison argues April 2026 was the inflection point when enterprise AI spending crossed from experimental line items to structural budget commitments, with Anthropic's Q2 revenue tracking to $10.9 billion and its first profitable quarter. For tech leaders, this isn't a trend to watch — it's a cost category that will crowd out discretionary spend before annual plans can absorb it.

TechCrunch — YouTube will now automatically label AI videos
YouTube is switching from creator-declared AI disclosure to autonomous detection: its internal systems will apply AI labels whenever they detect "significant photorealistic AI," make those labels more prominent across long-form and Shorts, and permanently lock labels on content made with YouTube's own tools (Veo, Dream Screen) even if creators dispute them. The precedent matters beyond YouTube — platform-level provenance enforcement, not self-certification, is becoming the industry's default approach to AI content trust.

MIT Technology Review — Google I/O showed how the path for AI-driven science is shifting
Google moved Nobel laureate John Jumper — the architect of AlphaFold — off science-specific AI tools and onto coding AI, a personnel decision that signals a strategic conviction that general agentic systems will eventually outperform domain-specific models for scientific discovery. The bet carries real risk: scientists in early testing describe Google's Co-Scientist as "consulting the oracle of Delphi," but pulling investment from specialized tools could hollow out a decade of purpose-built scientific AI progress.

Harvard Business Review — AI's Impact on SaaS Will Be Uneven. Here's What Leaders Need to Know.
The early-2026 "SaaSpocalypse" — a broad software selloff driven by the assumption that AI makes SaaS rebuildable internally — is real but overgeneralized; the article argues that SaaS with deep workflow integrations, network effects, or regulatory lock-in will survive while standalone productivity tools that AI can replicate in weeks are genuinely at risk. Leaders who treat all SaaS as equally threatened will over-invest in rebuilds while ignoring the categories actually worth defending.

item.title: World News — May 28, 2026
item.description:
CNBC — Trump opposes Russia or China taking Iran's highly enriched uranium
Trump stated on May 27 that he would not accept Iran transferring its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to Russia or China as part of any deal — a new constraint that eliminates the one compromise Iran has been most open to, since Tehran has refused to surrender its HEU directly to the United States. With Iran also insisting on control over the Strait of Hormuz and the nuclear issue now explicitly off the table for phase-one negotiations, the structural gap between the two sides is wider than Trump's "largely negotiated" framing has suggested.

NPR — A record-breaking heat wave is hitting Europe
London reached 95°F for the second consecutive day on May 27, with temperatures forecast to exceed 100°F across parts of France and Southern Europe by the weekend; seven deaths in France are already attributed to the heat, and rail disruptions at London Waterloo have exposed how little European infrastructure was built for sustained high temperatures in late spring. Scientists note that this level of heat arriving in May — not July — represents a qualitative shift, not merely an intensification, of the climate baseline.

Foreign Policy — Surviving a World Without Rules [FP Live, Mark Leonard]
Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, discussed his new book *Surviving Chaos: Geopolitics When the Rules Fail* in a May 27 FP Live conversation, arguing that global politics now divides between "architects" — the US and Europe, which try to reimpose established rule-based blueprints — and "artisans" like China, which adapt and repurpose whatever structures exist. The distinction explains why Western sanctions regimes keep leaking and why bilateral deals are replacing multilateral institutions across trade, security, and technology governance.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 28, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Managers Are Struggling to Keep Up with the AI Productivity Boom
AI has so dramatically accelerated execution speed — one manager quoted in the piece notes "every 30 minutes, someone creates something I have to look at" — that managers have become the new bottleneck; the authors (Liz Fosslien and Mollie West Duffy) argue the fix requires shifting from task-level oversight to strategic direction-setting and priority clarification, so that approval cycles don't cancel out the productivity gains AI creates. Organizations that don't restructure managerial roles to match the new execution tempo will lose the benefit of AI investment entirely.

Harvard Business Review — Research: As Careers Get Longer, Midcareer Work Needs to Change
As working lives extend into people's 70s, organizations are applying assumptions built for 30-year careers to 50- or 60-year careers — a structural mismatch that burns out midcareer employees at precisely the moment they reach peak leadership potential. The research argues that the problem isn't individual resilience but organizational design: most firms have no deliberate framework for midcareer reinvention, career pivots, or sustainable workload management across a multi-decade arc.

item.title: Wildcard — May 28, 2026
item.description:
Lenny's Newsletter — The AI paradox: More automation, more humans, more work (Dan Shipper)
Dan Shipper, co-founder of Every.to and a daily builder of AI-native products, argues that the "AI replaces workers" narrative inverts the actual dynamic: most substantive work is now happening inside Codex and Claude Code, but every agent still requires a human director at each decision point, making autonomous execution and human oversight more intertwined, not less. Shipper is "wildly bullish on PMs and designers" specifically because the proliferation of agentic workers creates more — not fewer — coordination, prioritization, and judgment calls that only experienced humans can make.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 27, 2026
item.description:
Import AI — Import AI 458: Reckoning with the Future; and a Singularity Story
Jack Clark publishes an extended essay and short story imagining what a positive singularity looks like—a deliberate exercise by a frontier practitioner in thinking through what we're actually building toward. For senior tech leaders, it's a rare artifact: a credible voice articulating a concrete vision of the destination, not just the journey.

Simon Willison's Blog — The Pressure
AI-assisted security reporting has begun overwhelming open-source maintainers: the curl project is being flooded with AI-generated vulnerability reports, many invalid, consuming maintainer time at a rate that threatens the project's sustainability. The pattern signals a structural problem—AI reduces the cost of filing reports but shifts the verification burden entirely to human maintainers.

MIT Technology Review — A Reality Check on the AI Jobs Hysteria
Despite years of warnings about AI-driven unemployment, there is currently scant empirical evidence that AI has had large-scale impact on U.S. labor markets—visible disruption is concentrated in early-career hiring, not in headline employment figures. Tech leaders calibrating workforce strategy need to separate the long-run structural shift from the present reality, where displacement is gradual and targeted.

TechCrunch — DuckDuckGo Installs Are Up 30% as Users Reject Being "Force-Fed" Google's AI Search
Google's overhaul replacing traditional blue-link results with an AI agent is driving measurable migration to DuckDuckGo, as users push back against AI-mandatory product changes they didn't choose. The product strategy lesson: AI integration that removes user agency generates defection, not delight.

item.title: World News — May 27, 2026
item.description:
NBC News — US and Iran Officials Signal Progress as Fragile Ceasefire Holds
Iran and the United States have agreed in principle on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and disposing of Iran's enriched uranium stockpile, with mediators working to extend the ceasefire by 60 days and establish a framework for permanent nuclear negotiations. Key sticking points remain on the timing of sanctions relief and control terms for the strategic waterway.

CNBC — Russia Tells Rubio: US Citizens Should Leave Kyiv Ahead of "Systematic" Strikes
Russia warned that systematic strikes on Kyiv are planned in response to Ukraine's attack in Luhansk, with Foreign Minister Lavrov delivering the message directly to Secretary of State Rubio. The escalation comes as Trump and Zelenskyy are reportedly 90–95% aligned on a peace proposal, underscoring how military pressure continues in parallel with diplomatic progress.

Time — What to Know About Türkiye's Deepening Democratic Crisis
Turkish police raided the CHP opposition party headquarters using tear gas and rubber bullets, ejecting its elected leadership after a court annulled the 2023 party leadership vote—escalating a crackdown that includes the imprisonment of presidential candidate Ekrem İmamoğlu since March 2025. The pattern signals Erdoğan's government is prepared to use judicial and security apparatus to eliminate organized political opposition before the next electoral cycle.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 27, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That's Risky.
More than half of surveyed knowledge workers are turning to AI for career advice, emotional support, and social interaction, even as they report feeling lonely at work—creating a hidden erosion of the human connection that drives engagement and retention. Leaders who treat AI adoption as a productivity story while ignoring its social effects will face a compounding engagement problem that doesn't surface in usage metrics.

Harvard Business Review — The Best Leaders Embrace the Role of Supporting Character
Research from Stanford psychologist Jamil Zaki shows that leaders who practice intellectual humility—asking questions rather than broadcasting answers, and connecting employee work to personal values—produce measurably higher satisfaction, performance, and loyalty. In an environment where AI increasingly handles intellectual heavy lifting, the differentiating leadership move is curiosity and facilitation, not expertise.

item.title: Wildcard — May 27, 2026
item.description:
AMD Newsroom — AMD Announces Production Ramp of Next-Generation EPYC Processor "Venice" on TSMC 2nm
AMD has begun production of the first 2nm chip in the world—the EPYC "Venice"—designed specifically for agentic AI workloads, with 256 cores and a claimed 70% compute performance gain over the previous generation. This is the physical layer of the AI arms race becoming real: the compute substrate for the next generation of models is now in production.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 26, 2026
item.description:
Simon Willison's Weblog — Notes on Pope Leo XIV's encyclical on AI
Willison calls "Magnifica Humanitas"—Pope Leo XIV's 200-page AI encyclical released May 25—"some of the clearest writing on the ethics of integrating AI into modern society," highlighting sections on the interpretability problem (LLMs are "cultivated rather than built"), the risk of dependency weakening human creativity, and the call to "disarm AI" by removing it from unchecked military and corporate control. The Catholic Church's intervention draws explicitly on Rerum Novarum's 1891 labor-rights framework, giving policymakers in 90+ countries a morally-grounded vocabulary for AI regulation that is independent of technical debates about model safety.

MIT Technology Review — It's time to address the looming crisis in entry-level work
Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found workers aged 22–25 in AI-exposed roles (developers, CS reps, programmers) experienced a 16% relative employment decline after generative AI spread; MIT Technology Review argues firms are using AI to eliminate the junior tasks—drafting, triaging, summarizing—through which workers have traditionally acquired professional expertise. The short-term efficiency gain of AI substituting entry-level work may produce a capability drought 5–10 years out, as the apprenticeship pipeline that regenerates expert judgment is quietly hollowed out.

The Hacker News — 2026: The Year of AI-Assisted Attacks
Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 report shows AI has compressed the average time-to-exploit from 700 days in 2020 to 44 days in 2025, with 28.3% of CVEs now exploited within 24 hours of disclosure; frontier AI models reaching 81% on SWE-bench means the same models that write production code are now usable by unsophisticated attackers to build zero-day exploits at scale. Any vulnerability management program still calibrated to the old 700-day window is operating on a threat model that is structurally obsolete.

TechCrunch — The SpaceX IPO filing is filled with AI bets, Starship dreams, and Elon Musk at the center
SpaceX's S-1 filing—targeting a $1.75T valuation that would make it the largest IPO in history—reveals a strategy built on orbital AI data centers, the completed xAI merger, and executive pay packages tied to Mars colonization milestones, with a claimed $28T total addressable market. The orbital data center bet introduces a variable to compute strategy that no current roadmap accounts for: if SpaceX executes, the next competitive tier in AI infrastructure may be space-based.

item.title: World News — May 26, 2026
item.description:
CNBC — U.S. conducts 'self-defense strikes' in Iran as Trump pushes for peace deal
CENTCOM struck Iranian missile sites and naval vessels planting mines in the Strait of Hormuz on May 26 even as both sides say they've agreed on "a large portion" of a peace deal's terms, with Secretary Rubio calling the agreement "a pretty solid thing on the table" while Iran called the strikes a ceasefire violation. The pattern—military coercion running simultaneously with diplomatic progress—means Strait reopening is a matter of weeks rather than months, but each incident in the field carries an escalation risk that could collapse talks entirely.

Foreign Policy — Europe Rethinks American Ties as Trump Rages
After initially accommodating Trump with defense spending increases and bilateral economic concessions, European governments are building an independent security architecture through a British-French-led coalition of 35 nations—including Japan, Canada, and Australia—deliberately designed to function without U.S. leadership. For organizations whose technology partnerships, export compliance, and supply chain security rely on a coherent transatlantic order, this is the most significant structural shift in Western institutional architecture since NATO's founding.

NBC News — Kim Jong Un vows to continue support for Russia as North Korea opens memorial museum for troops killed in Ukraine war
North Korea opened a state memorial museum for soldiers killed fighting in Ukraine—attended by Russian Defense Minister Belousov—with Kim pledging that military cooperation will "advance nonstop," formalizing a partnership that has deployed up to 12,000 North Korean troops and returned them with advanced drone warfare experience. The memorial institutionalizes the alliance in domestic propaganda, making reversal politically costly and permanently altering the security calculus on the Korean Peninsula.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 26, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — "Listen for the Silence": Insights from a Long-Serving CEO
Aflac CEO Dan Amos describes his operating model as "consultant-in-chief"—delegating decisions to those with the best information while staying most attuned to what his team avoids raising rather than what they do raise. In organizations where AI is changing what work looks like faster than management reporting can track, the habit of listening for silence—noticing what topics subordinates aren't surfacing—is the most reliable early-warning system for the problems most likely to become crises.

Harvard Business Review — Why Effective Leaders Get Branded as Problems
Luis Velasquez identifies four sources of the friction that labels effective leaders as organizational problems: capability gaps, perception mismatches (accurate work, misread intent), identity incongruence (right skills, wrong context), and system misalignment (individual is fine, the org is broken). For a senior leader managing high-performers generating organizational friction, the diagnostic framework matters more than any intervention—treating a system misalignment as a capability gap makes the problem worse.

item.title: Wildcard — May 26, 2026
item.description:
TechCrunch — The pope's AI encyclical isn't really about AI
TechCrunch's analysis of "Magnifica Humanitas" argues the encyclical's core subject is the concentration of economic and political power in a small elite—AI is the contemporary occasion, but the document's concerns (inequality, democratic erosion, labor displacement) would be recognizable to readers of Rerum Novarum in 1891, and the Pope presented it alongside Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah. Reading it as a power critique rather than an AI policy document explains its regulatory traction: it gives policymakers a morally-grounded framework for constraining Big Tech that doesn't require engaging technical debates about model capability.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 25, 2026
item.description:
Anthropic — Project Glasswing Finds Over 10,000 Critical Software Flaws in Its First Month
Anthropic's AI-powered security initiative, using its unreleased Mythos model, uncovered more than 10,000 vulnerabilities across launch partners in its first month—including 2,000 bugs at Cloudflare and a tenfold jump in Firefox fixes at Mozilla compared to prior Claude models. With AWS, Apple, Cisco, Microsoft, and NVIDIA all enrolled, this is the first large-scale proof that frontier AI can deliver order-of-magnitude productivity gains in a high-stakes enterprise function.

TechCrunch — OpenAI Co-Founder Andrej Karpathy Joins Anthropic's Pre-Training Team
Karpathy starts this week at Anthropic building a team that uses Claude to accelerate pre-training research—the work responsible for giving Claude its core knowledge and capabilities. Coming as Anthropic closes a $30 billion funding round and posts its first profitable quarter, this hire concentrates an unusual density of foundational AI talent at a single lab.

TechCrunch — Everyone Is Navigating AI Security in Real Time — Even Google
Security teams face a structural deficit: qualified professionals are scarce while AI-introduced vulnerabilities multiply faster than organizations can respond, and LinkedIn's CISO says sustainable AI security understanding is still years away. New research shows a properly revoked API key can still be exploited for up to 23 minutes due to gradual propagation in revocation systems—a concrete illustration of how AI infrastructure assumptions create unexpected attack surfaces.

MIT Technology Review — Three Things in AI to Watch, According to a Nobel-Winning Economist
Daron Acemoglu (Nobel 2024 Economics) identifies three AI developments worth closest scrutiny and warns that much influential AI economic research comes from companies with financial stakes in favorable conclusions. His core contrarian thesis—that AI's productivity impact will be modest because app usability hasn't matched raw capability—remains the most credible bearish case in a field dominated by vendor-driven optimism.

item.title: World News — May 25, 2026
item.description:
Bloomberg — US and Iran Inch Closer to a Deal to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran and the US have agreed to broad principles for an MOU that would see the strait reopen gradually in parallel with the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, with 60 days of negotiations to follow on sanctions relief and frozen assets. Partial resolution would immediately reduce energy prices and shipping costs globally, with direct implications for supply chains and inflation in technology-dependent sectors.

NPR — Russia Uses Hypersonic Oreshnik Missile in Mass Attack on Kyiv
Russia launched 600 drones and 90 missiles—including an Oreshnik hypersonic ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead—at Kyiv overnight, killing 2, injuring 77, and damaging 300 sites including the Chernobyl museum. The first combat use of the Oreshnik against a civilian capital crosses an escalatory threshold and directly complicates any diplomatic path toward a ceasefire.

Foreign Affairs — The War That Remade the Middle East
Fantappie and Nasr argue that the Iran war has permanently disrupted the Gulf's security architecture, forcing Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states to reassess decades-old assumptions about US protection guarantees, nuclear ambitions, and hedging between Washington and Beijing. Understanding this realignment is essential for anticipating energy markets, US-China competition in the region, and the shape of any post-conflict Gulf order.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 25, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — How to Build a Superteam That Keeps Getting Better
In periods of rapid change, the teams that outperform aren't those with the best plans or the most talent but those that learn fastest—by encouraging experimentation even when things go well, surfacing problems early, and investing in growth without requiring immediate payoff. As AI reshapes team composition and eliminates routine tasks, this reframes the central leadership challenge from managing talent to building learning velocity.

Farnam Street — Intelligence vs. Wisdom
The May 24 Brain Food letter centers on a single clean distinction: intelligence is getting what you want, wisdom is wanting what's worth getting in the first place. High-output people apply this by being maniacal about removing what others tolerate—which in an era of AI-amplified output makes the judgment of what to work on the decisive leadership variable.

item.title: Wildcard — May 25, 2026
item.description:
NPR — China Launches Shenzhou 23 Spacecraft; One Astronaut Set for Yearlong Stay
China launched three astronauts to the Tiangong station—including Lai Ka-ying, the first astronaut from Hong Kong—with one crew member assigned to a year-long mission studying human adaptability in sustained spaceflight. China's Tiangong program is now a mature, regularly crewed operation systematically building the physiological and operational data needed for extended missions beyond Earth orbit.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 24, 2026
item.description:
Bloomberg — Anthropic to Close Over $30 Billion Round as Soon as Next Week
Anthropic is set to close a funding round exceeding $30 billion at a pre-money valuation above $900 billion — surpassing OpenAI as the world's most valuable private AI company — with the close expected within days. The valuation more than doubled from $380 billion in February, reflecting investor conviction that the commercial inflection has arrived: Anthropic is projecting $10.9 billion in Q2 revenue and its first operating profit.

OpenAI — An OpenAI Model Has Disproved a Central Conjecture in Discrete Geometry
A general-purpose OpenAI reasoning model independently disproved Paul Erdős's unit distance conjecture — unsolved since 1946 — discovering an infinite family of point arrangements that beat the previous best construction using algebraic number theory, verified by external mathematicians. This is the first time a general-purpose AI (not a math-specialized system) has produced novel, externally-verified mathematical results, marking a shift from AI as tool to AI as scientific contributor.

TechCrunch — Trump Delays AI Security Executive Order, Saying Language "Could Have Been a Blocker"
Trump postponed signing an executive order on AI security after last-minute objections, saying he didn't want any provision to "get in the way" of American AI leadership over China. The delay signals that US AI policy remains subordinated to competitive dynamics rather than safety frameworks — a variable tech leaders should factor into compliance planning and product roadmaps.

Cosmos Institute — The 2026 Cosmos Lecture: Jack Clark on Human Autonomy
Anthropic co-founder and Import AI author Jack Clark, speaking at Oxford, argued that the central challenge ahead is not AI capability but preserving human cognitive autonomy — and predicted a 60%+ probability of recursive AI self-improvement (an AI model training its own successor) by 2028. The accompanying essay makes the case that autonomy must be actively designed for, not assumed to survive.

item.title: World News — May 24, 2026
item.description:
NPR — Trump: Deal with Iran Is "Largely Negotiated"
Trump announced on social media that an agreement to end the Iran war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz is "largely negotiated" and will be announced shortly — but Iran's top negotiator simultaneously declared Tehran "will not compromise," with outstanding disputes including nuclear enrichment, sanctions relief, and reparations. If the Strait reopens, fuel prices and global supply chains disrupted since the conflict began would materially improve.

CNBC — Taiwan and China Coast Guards in Standoff at Top of South China Sea
Taiwan and China's coast guards entered a second day of standoff near the Pratas Islands — 400km from Taiwan, widely seen as its most vulnerable territory — with China using unusual sovereignty language and holding an extended position that Taiwan officials called unprecedented in both wording and duration. The standoff follows Xi Jinping's direct warning to Trump at the Beijing summit that mishandling Taiwan would put the US-China relationship "in great jeopardy."

Foreign Policy — Trump Orders 5,000 U.S. Troops to Poland, Reversing Hegseth Decision
Weeks after Defense Secretary Hegseth canceled a troop deployment to Poland, Trump reversed course and ordered 5,000 troops restored to NATO's eastern flank — leaving allies publicly grateful but privately rattled by Washington's erratic signaling. The episode illustrates the structural instability in US commitments to European partners that is accelerating Europe's drive for independent defense capacity.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 24, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Beware the Agentic Convergence Trap
When companies deploy AI agents trained on the same market data, optimizing similar objectives at machine speed, their independent systems converge on identical decisions — eroding differentiation and, in some cases, inviting regulatory scrutiny for implicit collusion. The article identifies the trap's mechanism and offers design principles for leaders who need competitive differentiation to survive agentic AI deployment.

Harvard Business Review — It's Hard to Use AI as a Team. These 3 Practices Can Help.
A five-month study found that without deliberate design, AI integration reduces team engagement, narrows participation in meetings, and shifts ownership from the collective to individual power users. Teams that avoided the failure mode engaged AI at the group level, assigned it multiple personas to deepen discussion, and maintained joint ownership of prompts and outputs.

item.title: Wildcard — May 24, 2026
item.description:
OpenAI — How Frontier Firms Are Pulling Ahead (B2B Signals)
OpenAI's large-scale, privacy-preserving analysis of enterprise usage finds that frontier firms use 3.5x as much intelligence per worker as typical firms — up from 2x a year ago — and the gap is widest in agentic workflows, where frontier firms send 16x as many Codex messages. The core finding: most of the frontier advantage comes not from having access to AI but from depth of use across more task types, not from message volume alone.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 23, 2026
item.description:
The Batch (DeepLearning.AI) — Hermes vs. OpenClaw, Cybersecurity Alarms Ring, More-Interactive Conversations, Can Agents Do Human Work?
Issue 354 covers the rise of Hermes as a rival to the wildly popular OpenClaw autonomous agent, the UK AI Security Institute's finding that Claude Mythos Preview and GPT-5.5 can reliably execute attacks that would take humans three hours, and benchmark analysis showing agent performance is concentrated in software engineering and mathematical occupations. The convergence of autonomous capability and offensive security potential in the same model generation is the development tech leaders need to track.

Fortune — The big questions OpenAI's trillion-dollar IPO filing may finally answer
OpenAI confidentially filed its S-1 with the SEC on May 22, targeting a Q4 2026 public listing at a valuation between $852 billion and $1 trillion; Q1 revenue was $5.7 billion, but the company posted a negative 122% operating margin — losing $1.22 for every dollar earned. The filing is the first formal financial disclosure of frontier AI's true cost structure, and the numbers will force a hard reset on how the market prices AI infrastructure and vendor lock-in.

The Hacker News — GitHub Internal Repositories Breached via Malicious Nx Console VS Code Extension
Attackers published a trojanized version of the Nx Console VS Code extension for 18 minutes on May 18, long enough to steal credentials and exfiltrate 3,800 internal GitHub repositories; the same wave separately compromised Microsoft's Python SDK on PyPI. Every engineering organization that allows unvetted VS Code extension installs is exposed to this attack class, and the incident establishes developer toolchains as a primary attack surface equal to any other privileged access vector.

Simon Willison's Weblog — Datasette Agent
Simon Willison released Datasette Agent, an extensible AI assistant embedded directly in the Datasette data exploration tool, enabling natural-language queries, multi-step analysis, and tool-chaining against connected databases. The release is a practical demonstration of a broader pattern: AI agents are moving from standalone applications into the fabric of existing developer tools, changing how data infrastructure will be designed and used.

item.title: World News — May 23, 2026
item.description:
NPR — Rubio arrives in India ahead of Quad talks as U.S. tries to reset strained ties
Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Saturday for a visit that will include a Quad Foreign Ministers' Meeting with counterparts from Australia and Japan — the first senior U.S. visit since tariff disputes and diverging positions on Russia cooled the bilateral relationship. The meeting tests whether the Indo-Pacific alignment can hold under Trump's transactional foreign policy at the same moment China is escalating economic and military pressure on Japan and Taiwan.

PBS NewsHour — U.S. military boards Iranian-flagged oil tanker suspected of trying to breach blockade
A U.S. Navy vessel boarded an Iranian-flagged tanker in the Gulf of Oman attempting to break the American blockade, with both sides maintaining a dual blockade of the Persian Gulf while Iran charges vessels over $1 million per transit in strait tolls. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed — it carries roughly 20% of global oil — and the shutdown is on track to produce a European energy crisis comparable to the 2022 Russia-Ukraine shock.

AEI — China & Taiwan Update, May 22, 2026
President Trump signaled that U.S. arms sales to Taiwan are under active consideration as a "negotiating chip" with Beijing, and the WHO rejected Taiwan's participation in the World Health Assembly for the tenth consecutive year. China is simultaneously escalating economic and rhetorical pressure on Japan over Tokyo's remilitarization, tightening the web of coercion across the Indo-Pacific at precisely the moment U.S. commitment to regional allies is most uncertain.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 23, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — How to Move from AI Experimentation to AI Transformation
Companies deploying AI are falling into the "micro-productivity trap": optimizing individual tasks and generating isolated efficiency gains that never translate into measurable business outcomes because the underlying workflows remain unchanged. Moving from experimentation to transformation requires redesigning what work gets done, not just how fast existing work moves — a fundamentally different mandate than purchasing AI licenses.

Harvard Business Review — Data Privacy Is a Growth Strategy
A 14-year study analyzing 360 real-world corporate privacy announcements found that markets consistently reward firms that invest in privacy practices, with strong-privacy brands seeing a 12.31% increase in customer patronage — with the effect amplified for companies that had experienced a prior breach. For technology leaders managing customer data, this reframes privacy investment from compliance overhead into a measurable competitive lever with quantifiable return.

item.title: Wildcard — May 23, 2026
item.description:
Brookings Institution — Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
A survey of the academic literature on AI's labor market effects finds the evidence fundamentally inconclusive: studies show both reduced unemployment and declining job postings in AI-exposed occupations, and the timing of shifts correlates more closely with macroeconomic cycles than with ChatGPT's release. Leaders building workforce forecasts on AI disruption narratives should know the empirical research cannot yet distinguish AI effects from coincident macro factors.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 22, 2026
item.description:
TechCrunch — Anthropic says it's about to have its first profitable quarter
Anthropic will deliver its first operating profit on approximately $10.9 billion in Q2 2026 revenue—more than doubling its prior quarter—while cautioning that profitability may not persist as large compute commitments hit later in the year. The result confirms that a safety-first AI lab can reach commercial scale without the economics of frontier AI becoming the exclusive province of tech giants with existing platform distribution.

TechCrunch — OpenAI barrels toward IPO that may happen in September
OpenAI is confidentially filing its IPO prospectus with the SEC as early as today, targeting a September public debut at a valuation above $1 trillion, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters. The filing will generate the first public pricing signal for frontier AI revenue multiples, setting the benchmark that will govern every subsequent AI company valuation, M&A deal, and employee equity expectation in the sector.

TechCrunch — Google is pitching an AI agent ecosystem to consumers who may not buy it
Google's information agents—a 24/7 AI-powered reinvention of Google Alerts that monitors topics autonomously in the background—and the Gemini Spark personal agent are currently limited to $100/month Ultra subscribers, and post-I/O analysis finds the agent-as-background-service proposition lacks a clear consumer value narrative. The gap between the technical capability Google demonstrated and consumer willingness to pay for persistent autonomous AI is the most consequential adoption question of the next 12 months, because mass-market agent uptake is the load-bearing assumption in every agentic AI roadmap across the industry.

TechCrunch — AI search startups are blowing up
Exa Labs raised $250 million at a $2.2 billion valuation—tripling its prior valuation in under a year—and joins Tavily, Parallel Web Systems, and TinyFish as well-capitalized challengers building AI-native search infrastructure as Google's own pivot away from link-based search creates a structural window for new entrants. For any organization whose web traffic, SEO, and content distribution strategy still assumes Google-indexed search as the default information retrieval layer, this capital concentration in alternatives signals that assumption is now actively contested.

item.title: World News — May 22, 2026
item.description:
CNBC — U.S., Iran signal peace progress — but remain at odds over enriched uranium, Strait of Hormuz tolls
Two months into the U.S.-Iran war, both sides say gaps have "reduced," but Secretary of State Rubio declared any deal "unfeasible" if Iran pursues permanent toll control of the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington's demand that Iran surrender its enriched uranium stockpile remains Tehran's core negotiating red line. Until those two gaps close—and no current mechanism exists for closing them—energy market volatility remains structurally elevated and any planning assumption of near-term resolution is not supported by the current negotiating record.

Foreign Policy — Why the Quad Was Doomed From the Start
As Secretary Rubio heads to India for a Quad foreign-ministers meeting starting May 23, Foreign Policy argues the Quad's structural defect is a fundamental divergence between U.S. and Indian interests on China: Washington treats China as an adversary to contain while New Delhi treats it as a neighbor to manage. For tech and business leaders who depend on the U.S.-India technology partnership as a stable geopolitical assumption—in semiconductor supply chains, defense tech cooperation, or AI research alliances—the Quad's continued failure to hold a leaders' summit signals that institutional backing is weaker than the partnership's public profile suggests.

NPR — Ebola fears surge on the ground in Congo over rapid spread of a rare type
Congo's Ebola outbreak—driven by the Bundibugyo variant, for which there is no approved vaccine—has exceeded 600 suspected cases and 139 deaths, spread to Uganda, infected an American now hospitalized in Germany, and prompted WHO to declare a global health emergency. A PHEIC in one of the world's most conflict-affected regions, where armed groups actively impede the health response and a vaccine is six to nine months away, represents a material travel and operations risk for any organization with supply chains or personnel in Central or East Africa.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 22, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Negotiating When There Is No Plan B
When facing one-sided dependency or "take it or leave it" ultimatums, negotiators can create leverage by identifying partial or temporary alternatives, reframing threats as warnings, appealing to fairness norms, and seeking tacit rather than explicit consent—a practical expansion of the BATNA framework for asymmetric negotiations. The scenarios the article addresses—vendor lock-in, sole-source contracts, regulatory dependencies—are precisely the negotiation contexts that AI compute concentration and platform consolidation are creating for senior tech leaders right now.

Lenny's Newsletter — How to build a company that withstands any era | Eric Ries, Lean Startup author
Eric Ries's new book Incorruptible argues that companies self-corrupt not through bad actors but through "financial gravity"—the structural pull toward short-term optimization—and that the reliable countermeasure is governance design (charters, purpose trusts, mission-protection clauses), not culture, because values erode under pressure while structure holds. The interview draws on examples from Anthropic, Costco, and Novo Nordisk to show that the companies which survive competitive intensity and generational leadership transitions share a design decision made early and rarely revisited: they built structures that resist optimization pressure, not just people who intended to resist it.

item.title: Wildcard — May 22, 2026
item.description:
Air Street Press — State of AI: May 2026
Four Chinese AI labs—Z.ai (GLM-5.1), MiniMax (M2.7), Moonshot (Kimi K2.6), and DeepSeek (V4)—released open-weights coding models within a 12-day window, all converging on the same capability ceiling on agentic engineering benchmarks at meaningfully lower inference cost than Western frontier models. The pattern is the second such rapid multi-lab Chinese release in six months, confirming that the Western frontier advantage in coding and agentic tasks is narrowing faster than public competitive analysis typically reflects.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 21, 2026
item.description:
TechCrunch — Anthropic will pay xAI $1.25B per month for compute
Anthropic's agreement to lease all of xAI's Colossus 1 data center (220,000+ GPUs) for $1.25 billion per month—disclosed in SpaceX's S-1 SEC filing—reveals the full scale of the AI industry's compute dependency, with the deal potentially worth $40B+ through 2029. Frontier model companies are now structurally beholden to whoever controls the GPU clusters, and that leverage sits with a direct competitor.

TechCrunch — Elon Musk has lost his lawsuit against Sam Altman and OpenAI
A California jury dismissed all of Musk's claims in under two hours on statute-of-limitations grounds, never ruling on whether OpenAI's conversion to a for-profit entity violated its original charitable mission. The verdict clears an immediate legal obstacle to OpenAI's ongoing restructuring, but Musk has pledged to appeal and the governance question remains live.

TechCrunch — Google updates its Gemini app to take on ChatGPT and Claude at IO 2026
Google launched Gemini Spark at I/O—a 24/7 personal AI agent that operates continuously in the background, executing tasks without user prompts, alongside a new Gemini Omni video model and redesigned interface. Google is pivoting from chatbot to always-on agent, making the same architectural bet as OpenAI's Operator: that persistent autonomous execution, not query-response, is the next platform.

TechCrunch — Google just declared itself a contender in AI design at IO 2026
Google announced Pics, an AI-powered design and image-generation app for Workspace that generates marketing materials, graphics, and mock-ups from text prompts, placing it in direct competition with Adobe, Figma, and Canva. Google is using its enterprise distribution to enter the creative software market at exactly the moment AI is unbundling every workflow tool in that category.

item.title: World News — May 21, 2026
item.description:
NPR — Putin and Xi hail their friendship and growing energy trade at meeting in Beijing
Putin and Xi signed 40+ cooperation agreements in Beijing just days after Trump's own summit with Xi, with bilateral trade at $228 billion and Russian oil exports to China up 35% in Q1 2026. China is simultaneously deepening ties with both Washington and Moscow, positioning itself as an indispensable node in global order rather than a side-choosing ally.

NBC News — Ukraine ally Britain eases new sanctions on Russian oil as fuel prices surge over Iran war
The UK delayed new Russian oil sanctions because the Strait of Hormuz closure has driven fuel prices high enough to create a domestic cost-of-living squeeze. The Iran war is now indirectly relieving economic pressure on Russia—the same Western allies who pledged to isolate Moscow are being compelled to ease that isolation to manage their own energy economics.

Foreign Policy — Ukraine Has a New War Strategy Against Russia—and It's Working
Ukraine's long-range drone campaign targeting Russian oil refineries and port infrastructure has cut seaborne oil exports by ~300,000 barrels per day and driven refinery output to its lowest since 2009, offsetting Western diplomatic backsliding on sanctions. Ukraine is demonstrating that sustained economic targeting of energy infrastructure can substitute for diplomatic leverage when allied political will proves unreliable.

item.title: Leadership & Strategy — May 21, 2026
item.description:
Harvard Business Review — Supporting Your Employees' Career Growth When Everyone Is Overwhelmed
As AI disruption and economic instability render traditional career ladders irrelevant, the practical alternative is embedding development into daily work—shifting conversations from long-term advancement to near-term skill acquisition. Reframing growth from "where are you going" to "what are you learning this quarter" improves retention without requiring the organizational stability that no longer exists.

Farnam Street — The Microscope and The Telescope
The most effective performers allocate roughly 90% of attention to the microscope (daily execution) and only occasionally consult the telescope (multi-year vision), rather than splitting attention evenly between near and far. Sustained long-range focus without proportional daily execution produces elaborate plans that never compound into results.

item.title: Wildcard — May 21, 2026
item.description:
MIT Technology Review — Colossal Biosciences is growing chickens in a 3D-printed artificial eggshell
Colossal Biosciences hatched 26 live chicks from fully artificial eggs—3D-printed lattices coated with a silicone membrane that replicates the gas-exchange function of a natural shell—as a technical proving step toward reviving the dodo and giant moa. The breakthrough demonstrates that synthetic biology is advancing faster than public debate about de-extinction ethics has materialized.

item.title: AI & Technology — May 20, 2026
item.description:
Import AI — Import AI 457: AI stuxnet; cursed Muon optimizer; and positive alignment
Jack Clark examines fast16.sys, a 20-year-old malware that silently corrupts high-precision industrial calculations without detection, and uses it to argue that a future superintelligence might pursue "AI non-proliferation" by quietly sabotaging competing systems the way nuclear states guard against nuclear proliferation. The issue also proposes "positive alignment" as a design target—building AI systems not merely safe but actively supportive of human flourishing—a framing that is starting to appear in serious policy circles.

Simon Willison's Weblog — Gemini 3.5 Flash: more expensive, but Google plan to use it for everything
Google launched Gemini 3.5 Flash at I/O 2026 as its strongest model yet for coding and autonomous agents—faster than comparable frontier models and better across nearly all benchmarks than its predecessor—while simultaneously announcing it as the universal substrate for all Google products. The strategic tell is in the name: unlike prior "Flash" models positioned as cheap alternatives, this one is more expensive, signaling that Google is collapsing its model tiers rather than maintaining a cost/quality ladder.

TechCrunch — Google Search as you know it is over
At I/O 2026, Google unveiled the biggest overhaul to Search in 25 years: an "intelligent search box" fronting persistent AI agents that monitor topics autonomously around the clock instead of responding only when prompted. The shift from query-response to continuous information service has direct consequences for web traffic, SEO strategy, and how enterprises should architect their content and information retrieval systems.

OpenAI — OpenAI launches the OpenAI Deployment Company
OpenAI launched a $4 billion majority-owned deployment arm backed by 19 firms—Bain, TPG, Goldman Sachs, SoftBank, and others—designed to embed "Forward Deployed Engineers" directly inside enterprise organizations to redesign workflows around AI. The move is a structural pivot from selling API access to owning AI implementation, putting OpenAI in direct competition with the consulting and systems-integration firms now funding it.

item.title: World News — May 20, 2026
item.description:
CNBC — Putin heads to Beijing days after Trump in test of China's balancing act
Putin arrived in Beijing on May 19 for a two-day state visit—his 25th trip to China—just five days after Trump's summit with Xi, with both sides issuing a joint statement warning against a return to the "law of the jungle" and opposing Trump's $175B Golden Dome missile defense program. China hosting the leaders of both the United States and Russia within six days is the clearest public demonstration yet of Beijing's strategy: engage both powers simultaneously while binding itself to neither.

NPR — Drone strikes UAE nuclear plant highlighting risk of renewed war
Three drones entered UAE airspace targeting the Barakah nuclear plant—the Arab world's only nuclear power station—with one breaching air defenses and igniting a fire outside the inner perimeter; the IAEA chief called it an "unacceptable" attack on nuclear infrastructure. The incident, set against a fragile U.S.-Iran ceasefire and an International Energy Agency assessment that the conflict has caused the largest oil supply disruption in the market's history, signals that Gulf energy infrastructure is now an active military target.

CBS News — Iran more than doubled executions in 2025 as global use of death penalty hit 44-year high
Amnesty International's annual report records 2,707 state executions in 2025—a 78% increase from 2024 and the highest figure since 1981—with Iran accounting for at least 2,159 of them, more than double its prior-year total, driven primarily by drug offenses and political suppression. For leaders tracking the Iran conflict, the data provides a quantified measure of the regime's internal posture at precisely the moment it is engaged in military hostilities with the United States.
